Divergences and Dual Norms

This chapter compares optimal transport with divergence-based and adversarial ways of measuring discrepancy. The main stake is topological: ϕ\phiϕ-divergences are cheap but strong, while dual norms and GAN objectives can be weak enough to compare singular measures. The discussion connects classical information divergences Ciszár, 1967Ali & Silvey, 1966 with modern integral probability metrics and generative modeling Sriperumbudur et al., 2009Goodfellow et al., 2014Arjovsky et al., 2017.

Guiding Comparison

Dual norms and integral probability metrics compare measures through test functions. Phi-divergences compare them through density ratios. This single change explains most of the chapter: test-function discrepancies can be weak enough to compare singular measures, while ratio-based divergences are often cheap and statistically classical but topologically strong.

Dual Norms and Integral Probability Metrics¶

This section isolates the test-function viewpoint behind weak discrepancies. Dual norms generalize the W1\Wass_1W1​ test-function principle and are useful in statistics because they compare distributions through a restricted discriminator class.

Integral Probability Metrics¶

The Kantorovich--Rubinstein formula for W1\Wass_1W1​ is a special case of a dual norm. This viewpoint designs weak discrepancies by testing signed differences of measures against a controlled class of functions.

Definition: Dual Seminorm and Integral Probability Metric

Let BBB be a nonempty symmetric convex class of measurable functions that are integrable against the measures under consideration. For a signed measure ξ\xiξ, define the extended dual seminorm

∥ξ∥B:=sup⁡f∈B∫Xf(x)  dξ(x).\norm{\xi}_B \eqdef \sup_{f\in B} \int_\X f(x)\,\d\xi(x).∥ξ∥B​:=f∈Bsup​∫X​f(x)dξ(x).
(1)

It is a norm when it is finite and BBB separates signed measures. Applied to α−β\alpha-\betaα−β, it is an integral probability metric; it is a genuine metric precisely when BBB separates probability measures.

Symmetry makes the supremum equal to sup⁡f∈B∣∫f  dξ∣\sup_{f\in B}|\int f\,\d\xi|supf∈B​∣∫fdξ∣, while convexity makes BBB a natural unit ball.

The choice of the test-function class BBB determines both the topology and the statistical behavior of the discrepancy Sriperumbudur et al., 2012Sriperumbudur et al., 2009Sriperumbudur et al., 2008.

Example: Total variation

As recalled in Definition Definition: Total Variation and Proposition Proposition: Dual And Measure Definitions Of Total Variation, total variation is the dual norm associated with the unit ball of continuous functions

B={f∈C(X)  :  ∥f∥∞≤1}.B = \enscond{f \in \Cc(\X)}{\norm{f}_\infty \leq 1}.B={f∈C(X):∥f∥∞​≤1}.
(2)

Total variation is the canonical nontrivial example of a discrepancy that is both a ϕ\phiϕ-divergence and a dual norm; see Sriperumbudur et al., 2009.

Example: W1\Wass_1W1​ norm

On zero-mass signed measures with finite first moment, the Kantorovich--Rubinstein norm underlying W1\Wass_1W1​ is the extended dual seminorm (1) associated with

B={f  :  Lip⁡(f)≤1}B = \enscond{f}{\Lip(f) \leq 1}B={f:Lip(f)≤1}
(3)

the set of 1-Lipschitz functions.

Example: Flat norm and Dudley metric

If BBB is uniformly bounded and separates measures, then ∥⋅∥B\norm{\cdot}_B∥⋅∥B​ is a finite norm on the whole space M(X)\Mm(\Xx)M(X) of finite signed measures.

This is not the case for W1\Wass_1W1​: zero total mass is necessary, and on an unbounded space a finite first moment is also required. For nonzero total mass, ∥ξ∥B=+∞\norm{\xi}_B=+\infty∥ξ∥B​=+∞ because constants belong to the Lipschitz ball.

This is remedied by imposing a bound on the value of the potential f\ff, which leads for instance to the flat norm,

B={f  :  Lip⁡(f)≤1and∥f∥∞≤1}.B=\enscond{f}{\Lip(f) \leq 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \norm{\f}_\infty \leq 1}.B={f:Lip(f)≤1and∥f∥∞​≤1}.
(4)

On compact metric spaces, it metrizes weak convergence of finite nonnegative measures, and weak-∗\ast∗ convergence on every total-variation-bounded family of signed measures.

The finite-dimensional version is obtained from the usual W1\Wass_1W1​ dual linear program by adding the box constraints ∣fk∣≤1\abs{\fD_k}\leq1∣fk​∣≤1.

The flat norm is sometimes called the “Kantorovich--Rubinstein” norm Hanin, 1992 and has been used as a fidelity term for inverse problems in imaging Lellmann et al., 2014.

The flat norm is equivalent to the bounded-Lipschitz, or Dudley, metric, whose test class is

B={f  :  Lip⁡(f)+∥f∥∞≤1}.B=\enscond{f}{\Lip(f) + \norm{f}_\infty \leq 1}.B={f:Lip(f)+∥f∥∞​≤1}.
(5)

On a Euclidean domain, Lip⁡(f)=∥∇f∥∞\Lip(f)=\norm{\nabla f}_\inftyLip(f)=∥∇f∥∞​ for differentiable fff.

The following proposition gives a compact-space criterion. The dual ball should be rich enough to approximate continuous observables, but compact enough for weak convergence to imply uniform convergence over the discriminator class.

Proposition: Metrization by Dual Norms

Assume that X\XX is compact, B=−BB=-BB=−B, and the measures considered are probability measures.

  1. If every function in C(X)\Cc(\X)C(X) can be uniformly approximated by elements of span⁡(B)\operatorname{span}(B)span(B), then ∥αn−α∥B→0\norm{\alpha_n-\alpha}_B\to0∥αn​−α∥B​→0 implies αn⇀α\alpha_n\rightharpoonup\alphaαn​⇀α.

  2. If B⊂C(X)B\subset\Cc(\X)B⊂C(X) is compact for ∥⋅∥∞\norm{\cdot}_\infty∥⋅∥∞​, then αn⇀α\alpha_n\rightharpoonup\alphaαn​⇀α implies ∥αn−α∥B→0\norm{\alpha_n-\alpha}_B\to0∥αn​−α∥B​→0.

Proof

For the first implication, ∥αn−α∥B→0\norm{\alpha_n-\alpha}_B\to0∥αn​−α∥B​→0 and the symmetry of BBB imply

∣∫f  d(αn−α)∣≤∥αn−α∥B(f∈B).\left|\int f\,\d(\alpha_n-\alpha)\right| \le \norm{\alpha_n-\alpha}_B \qquad (f\in B).∣∣​∫fd(αn​−α)∣∣​≤∥αn​−α∥B​(f∈B).
(6)

If h=∑j=1Jcjfj∈span⁡(B)h=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_jf_j\in\operatorname{span}(B)h=∑j=1J​cj​fj​∈span(B), then

∣∫h  d(αn−α)∣≤(∑j=1J∣cj∣)∥αn−α∥B,\left|\int h\,\d(\alpha_n-\alpha)\right| \le \left(\sum_{j=1}^J|c_j|\right)\norm{\alpha_n-\alpha}_B,∣∣​∫hd(αn​−α)∣∣​≤(j=1∑J​∣cj​∣)∥αn​−α∥B​,
(7)

so integrals converge for every h∈span⁡(B)h\in\operatorname{span}(B)h∈span(B). Let u∈C(X)u\in\Cc(\X)u∈C(X) and choose h∈span⁡(B)h\in\operatorname{span}(B)h∈span(B) with ∥u−h∥∞≤η\norm{u-h}_\infty\le\eta∥u−h∥∞​≤η. Since αn\alpha_nαn​ and α\alphaα are probabilities,

∣∫u  d(αn−α)∣≤∣∫h  d(αn−α)∣+2η.\left|\int u\,\d(\alpha_n-\alpha)\right| \le \left|\int h\,\d(\alpha_n-\alpha)\right| +2\eta .∣∣​∫ud(αn​−α)∣∣​≤∣∣​∫hd(αn​−α)∣∣​+2η.

Taking the limsup as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞ and then letting η→0\eta\to0η→0 gives weak convergence.

For the second implication, assume αn⇀α\alpha_n\rightharpoonup\alphaαn​⇀α and choose a subsequence (αnk)k(\alpha_{n_k})_k(αnk​​)k​ realizing the limsup of ∥αn−α∥B\norm{\alpha_n-\alpha}_B∥αn​−α∥B​. Since BBB is compact and f↦∫f  d(αnk−α)f\mapsto\int f\,\d(\alpha_{n_k}-\alpha)f↦∫fd(αnk​​−α) is continuous on BBB, the supremum is attained by some fnk∈Bf_{n_k}\in Bfnk​​∈B. Extract a further subsequence with fnk→ff_{n_k}\to ffnk​​→f uniformly. Then

∫fnk  d(αnk−α)=∫f  d(αnk−α)+∫(fnk−f)  dαnk−∫(fnk−f)  dα.\int f_{n_k}\,\d(\alpha_{n_k}-\alpha) = \int f\,\d(\alpha_{n_k}-\alpha) + \int (f_{n_k}-f)\,\d\alpha_{n_k} - \int (f_{n_k}-f)\,\d\alpha .∫fnk​​d(αnk​​−α)=∫fd(αnk​​−α)+∫(fnk​​−f)dαnk​​−∫(fnk​​−f)dα.

Corollary: Wasserstein Metrizes Weak Convergence

On a compact metric space, Wp\Wass_pWp​ metrizes weak convergence on probability measures for every p≥1p\ge1p≥1.

Proof

For p=1p=1p=1, take B={f:Lip⁡(f)≤1}B=\{f:\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1\}B={f:Lip(f)≤1}. The span of BBB contains all Lipschitz functions, which are dense in C(X)\Cc(\X)C(X) on compact metric spaces. This gives W1(αn,α)→0⇒αn⇀α\Wass_1(\alpha_n,\alpha)\to0\Rightarrow\alpha_n\rightharpoonup\alphaW1​(αn​,α)→0⇒αn​⇀α.

Conversely, constants do not change the pairing with αn−α\alpha_n-\alphaαn​−α. Fix x0∈Xx_0\in\Xx0​∈X and normalize potentials by f(x0)=0f(x_0)=0f(x0​)=0. The normalized unit Lipschitz ball is uniformly bounded by diam⁡(X)\operatorname{diam}(\X)diam(X) and equicontinuous, hence compact in ∥⋅∥∞\norm{\cdot}_\infty∥⋅∥∞​ by Arzela--Ascoli. The previous proposition gives W1(αn,α)→0\Wass_1(\alpha_n,\alpha)\to0W1​(αn​,α)→0. On compact spaces, all Wp\Wass_pWp​ distances induce the same topology.

Dual RKHS Norms and Maximum Mean Discrepancies¶

Kernel methods turn probability measures into mean elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The resulting Hilbertian dual seminorms are quadratic discrepancies, handled with Euclidean geometry while retaining a weak test-function interpretation.

Definition: Positive and Conditionally Positive Kernels

A symmetric function K:X×X→RK:\X\times\X\to\RRK:X×X→R is positive definite if for every n≥1n\ge1n≥1, every x1,…,xn∈Xx_1,\ldots,x_n\in\Xx1​,…,xn​∈X, and every r∈Rnr\in\RR^nr∈Rn,

∑i,j=1nrirjK(xi,xj)≥0.\sum_{i,j=1}^n r_i r_j K(x_i,x_j)\ge0.i,j=1∑n​ri​rj​K(xi​,xj​)≥0.
(10)

It is conditionally positive definite if the same inequality is required only for zero-sum vectors, ⟨r,1⟩=0\langle r,\mathbf{1}\rangle=0⟨r,1⟩=0.

Here ``positive definite’’ has its standard kernel-theory meaning of positive semidefinite. Strict positivity is an additional property, and its absence can make the induced discrepancy degenerate.

The conditional version is the right notion for probability distances, because one applies the quadratic form to signed measures ξ=α−β\xi=\alpha-\betaξ=α−β of total mass zero. Adding a(x)+a(y)a(x)+a(y)a(x)+a(y) to the kernel does not change ∬K(x,y)  dξ(x)  dξ(y)\iint K(x,y)\,\d\xi(x)\,\d\xi(y)∬K(x,y)dξ(x)dξ(y) on such measures, and many natural distance kernels are only conditionally positive definite.

Example: Riesz, energy and Matérn-type kernels

On Rd\RR^dRd, translation-invariant kernels are most transparent in Fourier variables. The Riesz family associated with (−Δ)−s(-\Delta)^{-s}(−Δ)−s has multiplier ∥ω∥−2s\norm{\om}^{-2s}∥ω∥−2s and defines a nonnegative quadratic form on zero-mass measures for which the low-frequency singularity is integrable; this is the kernel counterpart of classical Riesz potentials Berg et al., 1984. The energy distance corresponds to the conditionally positive kernel k(x,y)=−∥x−y∥\Krkhs(x,y)=-\norm{x-y}k(x,y)=−∥x−y∥, whose Fourier multiplier is proportional to ∥ω∥−(d+1)\norm{\om}^{-(d+1)}∥ω∥−(d+1); for ξ=α−β\xi=\al-\beξ=α−β,

−∬∥x−y∥ dξ(x) dξ(y)-\iint \norm{x-y}\d\xi(x)\d\xi(y)−∬∥x−y∥dξ(x)dξ(y)
(11)

is exactly the customary squared energy distance 2E∥X−Y∥−E∥X−X′∥−E∥Y−Y′∥2\EE\norm{X-Y}-\EE\norm{X-X'}-\EE\norm{Y-Y'}2E∥X−Y∥−E∥X−X′∥−E∥Y−Y′∥; only its Fourier representation carries a dimension-dependent constant Schoenberg, 1938Székely & Rizzo, 2004.

Shifted kernels replace (−Δ)−s(-\Delta)^{-s}(−Δ)−s by (−Δ+λI)−s(-\Delta+\lambda I)^{-s}(−Δ+λI)−s with λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. Their Fourier multiplier (∥ω∥2+λ)−s(\norm{\om}^2+\lambda)^{-s}(∥ω∥2+λ)−s is bounded at the origin, hence the kernel is positive definite without imposing zero mass. These are Matern kernels; in closed form they are radial and involve a modified Bessel function Wendland, 2005. The Laplacian kernel e−∥x−y∥/σe^{-\norm{x-y}/\sigma}e−∥x−y∥/σ is a low-smoothness Matern example, while the Gaussian kernel e−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2)e^{-\norm{x-y}^2/(2\sigma^2)}e−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2) is the infinite-smoothness limit after the usual rescaling of the Matern smoothness parameter.

Definition: Kernel Seminorm and MMD

Let KKK be positive definite. More generally, let KKK be conditionally positive definite and restrict attention to signed measures of total mass zero. For a signed measure ξ\xiξ with finite kernel energy, define

∥ξ∥K2:=∬X×XK(x,y)  dξ(x)  dξ(y).\norm{\xi}_K^2 \eqdef \iint_{\X\times\X}K(x,y)\,\d\xi(x)\,\d\xi(y).∥ξ∥K2​:=∬X×X​K(x,y)dξ(x)dξ(y).
(12)

For two probability measures, the maximum mean discrepancy associated with KKK is

MMD⁡K(α,β):=∥α−β∥K.\operatorname{MMD}_K(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \norm{\alpha-\beta}_K.MMDK​(α,β):=∥α−β∥K​.
(13)

It is a genuine distance when KKK is characteristic, meaning that zero MMD implies α=β\alpha=\betaα=β.

These seminorms are usually called maximum mean discrepancies in statistics and machine learning Gretton et al., 2012Muandet et al., 2017, and kernel norms in shape analysis Hofmann et al., 2008. For a positive-definite kernel, if X,X′X,X'X,X′ are independent with law α\alphaα, then ∥α∥K2=EX,X′(K(X,X′))\norm{\alpha}_K^2=\EE_{X,X'}(K(X,X'))∥α∥K2​=EX,X′​(K(X,X′)), whenever this expression is finite. For a conditionally positive kernel, fixing x0∈Xx_0\in\Xx0​∈X and replacing KKK by

K~(x,y)=K(x,y)−K(x,x0)−K(x0,y)+K(x0,x0)\widetilde K(x,y)=K(x,y)-K(x,x_0)-K(x_0,y)+K(x_0,x_0)K(x,y)=K(x,y)−K(x,x0​)−K(x0​,y)+K(x0​,x0​)
(14)

produces a positive-definite kernel with the same energy on zero-mass measures.

Proposition: Kernel Seminorm as an RKHS Dual Norm

Let H\mathcal{H}H be the RKHS with reproducing kernel KKK, and assume that the kernel mean embedding

mξ:=∫K(x,⋅)  dξ(x)m_\xi\eqdef\int K(x,\cdot)\,\d\xi(x)mξ​:=∫K(x,⋅)dξ(x)
(15)

is well-defined. Then

∥ξ∥K=sup⁡∥h∥H≤1∫h(x)  dξ(x),\norm{\xi}_K = \sup_{\norm{h}_{\mathcal{H}}\le1} \int h(x)\,\d\xi(x),∥ξ∥K​=∥h∥H​≤1sup​∫h(x)dξ(x),
(16)

so ∥⋅∥K\norm{\cdot}_K∥⋅∥K​ is the dual seminorm associated with the RKHS unit ball.

Proof

By the reproducing property,

∫h(x)  dξ(x)=⟨h,∫K(x,⋅)  dξ(x)⟩H=⟨h,mξ⟩H.\int h(x)\,\d\xi(x) = \left\langle h,\int K(x,\cdot)\,\d\xi(x) \right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} = \langle h,m_\xi\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}.∫h(x)dξ(x)=⟨h,∫K(x,⋅)dξ(x)⟩H​=⟨h,mξ​⟩H​.
(17)

Cauchy--Schwarz gives

sup⁡∥h∥H≤1∫h  dξ=∥mξ∥H.\sup_{\norm{h}_{\mathcal{H}}\le1}\int h\,\d\xi = \norm{m_\xi}_{\mathcal{H}}.∥h∥H​≤1sup​∫hdξ=∥mξ​∥H​.
(18)

Finally,

∥mξ∥H2=∬K(x,y)  dξ(x)  dξ(y).\norm{m_\xi}_{\mathcal{H}}^2 = \iint K(x,y)\,\d\xi(x)\,\d\xi(y).∥mξ​∥H2​=∬K(x,y)dξ(x)dξ(y).
(19)
Proposition: Universal Kernels Metrize Weak Convergence

Assume that X\XX is compact and that the RKHS generated by the continuous kernel KKK is dense in C(X)\Cc(\X)C(X) for the uniform norm. Then

MMD⁡K(αn,α)→0⟺αn⇀α\operatorname{MMD}_K(\alpha_n,\alpha)\to0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \alpha_n\rightharpoonup\alphaMMDK​(αn​,α)→0⟺αn​⇀α

If MMD⁡K(αn,α)→0\operatorname{MMD}_K(\alpha_n,\alpha)\to0MMDK​(αn​,α)→0, then for every g∈Hg\in\mathcal Hg∈H,

Further background on RKHS spaces can be found in Berlinet & Thomas-Agnan, 2003Hofmann et al., 2008Schölkopf & Smola, 2002.

Remark: Universal kernels

The hypothesis in Proposition Proposition: Universal Kernels Metrize Weak Convergence is called universality of the kernel. Equivalently, finite sums of the form ∑i=1naiK(xi,⋅)\sum_{i=1}^n a_i K(x_i,\cdot)∑i=1n​ai​K(xi​,⋅) are dense in C(X)\Cc(\X)C(X) for the uniform norm. For a bounded continuous translation-invariant kernel on Rd\RR^dRd, a standard sufficient condition is that its Bochner spectral measure have support equal to all of Rd\RR^dRd; under the usual C0C_0C0​ assumptions this characterizes C0C_0C0​-universality Sriperumbudur et al., 2008Sriperumbudur et al., 2012.

The preceding discrepancies are widely used as sample-based criteria, both for testing whether two populations agree and for evaluating generative models.

Example: Two-sample testing and generative-model evaluation

Given samples X1,…,Xn∼αX_1,\ldots,X_n\sim\alX1​,…,Xn​∼α and Y1,…,Ym∼βY_1,\ldots,Y_m\sim\beY1​,…,Ym​∼β, a two-sample test evaluates a statistic D(α^n,β^m)D(\hat\al_n,\hat\be_m)D(α^n​,β^​m​) under the null hypothesis H0:α=βH_0:\al=\beH0​:α=β. Wasserstein distances provide geometric choices of DDD, whereas MMD and the energy distance provide kernel and negative-type alternatives Ramdas et al., 2017Gretton et al., 2012Székely & Rizzo, 2004. In generative-model evaluation, the Frechet Inception Distance embeds the data in a neural feature space, fits a Gaussian to each empirical feature distribution, and computes the squared W2\Wass_2W2​ distance between these Gaussian laws: the squared distance between their empirical means plus the Bures covariance term of Proposition Proposition: Gaussian W2\Wass_2W2​ Formula And Bures Covariance Term Heusel et al., 2017. The Kernel Inception Distance instead estimates a squared MMD, typically with a polynomial kernel, in the same feature space Bińkowski et al., 2018. In both settings, the geometry encoded by DDD must be distinguished from the finite-sample calibration of D(α^n,β^m)D(\hat\al_n,\hat\be_m)D(α^n​,β^​m​); Sections Sample Complexity and Bias and Variance of OT analyze the resulting rates, bias and fluctuations.

In the special case where α=∑i=1naiδxi\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\delta_{x_i}α=∑i=1n​ai​δxi​​ is discrete, one obtains

∥α∥K2=∑i,i′aiai′K(xi,xi′)=a⊤KXa,\norm{\alpha}_K^2 = \sum_{i,i'} a_i a_{i'}K(x_i,x_{i'}) = a^\top K_X a,∥α∥K2​=i,i′∑​ai​ai′​K(xi​,xi′​)=a⊤KX​a,
(24)

where (KX)i,i′=K(xi,xi′)(K_X)_{i,i'}=K(x_i,x_{i'})(KX​)i,i′​=K(xi​,xi′​). Phi-Divergences¶

This section develops divergences based on pointwise density ratios. They are computationally simple and statistically classical, but on nondiscrete spaces they generally induce a topology much stronger than weak convergence and do not see small spatial displacements between mutually singular measures.

Definition by Density Ratios¶

On a common discrete support, phi-divergences cost only O(n)O(n)O(n) to evaluate, but on a continuous space they generally fail to metrize weak convergence. Bregman divergences provide a different convex construction and should not be conflated with density-ratio divergences.

Definition: Entropy Function

A function ϕ:R→R∪{+∞}\phi:\RR\to\RR\cup\{+\infty\}ϕ:R→R∪{+∞} is an entropy function if it is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, has domain contained in [0,+∞)[0,+\infty)[0,+∞), and dom⁡ϕ\operatorname{dom}\phidomϕ intersects (0,+∞)(0,+\infty)(0,+∞). Its growth at infinity is described by

ϕ∞′=lim⁡x→+∞ϕ(x)x∈R∪{+∞}.\phi'_\infty = \lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{\phi(x)}{x} \in \RR\cup\{+\infty\}.ϕ∞′​=x→+∞lim​xϕ(x)​∈R∪{+∞}.
(26)

If ϕ∞′=+∞\phi'_\infty=+\inftyϕ∞′​=+∞, then ϕ\phiϕ grows faster than any linear function and is called superlinear. Any entropy function induces a ϕ\phiϕ-divergence, also known as a Ciszar divergence or fff-divergence Ciszár, 1967Ali & Silvey, 1966.

Definition: ϕ\phiϕ-Divergence

Let ϕ\phiϕ be an entropy function and let α,β∈M+(X)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{M}_+(\X)α,β∈M+​(X). Write

α= dα dβ β+α⊥\alpha = \frac{\d\alpha}{\d\beta}\,\beta + \alpha^\perpα=dβdα​β+α⊥
(27)

be the Lebesgue decomposition of α\alphaα with respect to β\betaβ. The divergence is

Dϕ(α∣β):=∫Xϕ( dα dβ)  dβ+ϕ∞′ α⊥(X),D_\phi(\alpha|\beta) \eqdef \int_\X \phi\left(\frac{\d\alpha}{\d\beta}\right) \,\d\beta + \phi'_\infty\,\alpha^\perp(\X),Dϕ​(α∣β):=∫X​ϕ(dβdα​)dβ+ϕ∞′​α⊥(X),
(28)

with the convention 0⋅(+∞)=00\cdot(+\infty)=00⋅(+∞)=0, and extend it by +∞+\infty+∞ whenever either argument is not a nonnegative measure.

Here α⊥\alpha^\perpα⊥ is the part of α\alphaα singular with respect to β\betaβ. The singular term is the recession contribution of the perspective functional. It gives the weak-∗\ast∗ lower-semicontinuous extension of the density-ratio integral when singular mass appears. This is essential for linear-growth entropies such as total variation. For superlinear entropies, such as the usual entropy, ϕ∞′=+∞\phi'_\infty=+\inftyϕ∞′​=+∞, so the divergence is infinite when α\alphaα is not absolutely continuous with respect to β\betaβ.

For discrete measures supported on the same set,

α=∑iaiδxi,β=∑ibiδxi,\alpha=\sum_i a_i\delta_{x_i}, \qquad \beta=\sum_i b_i\delta_{x_i},α=i∑​ai​δxi​​,β=i∑​bi​δxi​​,
(29)

the formula becomes

Dϕ(a∣b)=∑i∈supp⁡(b)bi ϕ(aibi)+ϕ∞′∑i∉supp⁡(b)ai.D_\phi(a|b) = \sum_{i\in\operatorname{supp}(b)} b_i\, \phi\left(\frac{a_i}{b_i}\right) + \phi'_\infty \sum_{i\notin\operatorname{supp}(b)}a_i .Dϕ​(a∣b)=i∈supp(b)∑​bi​ϕ(bi​ai​​)+ϕ∞′​i∈/supp(b)∑​ai​.

Classical Examples and Topology¶

The following examples calibrate the strength of ϕ\phiϕ-divergences. KL is sensitive to absolute continuity, while total variation gives the strong topology and therefore behaves very differently from Wasserstein-type weak metrics.

Example: Kullback--Leibler divergence

The Kullback--Leibler divergence KL⁡:=DϕKL⁡\KL \eqdef \Divergm_{\phi_{\KL}}KL:=DϕKL​​, also known as the relative entropy, was already introduced in (21) and (11). It is the divergence associated to the Shannon--Boltzmann entropy function ϕKL⁡\phi_{\KL}ϕKL​, given by

ϕKL⁡(s)={slog⁡(s)−s+1for s>0,1for s=0,+∞otherwise.\phi_{\KL}(s)= \begin{cases} s\log(s)-s+1 & \textnormal{for } s>0 , \\ 1 & \textnormal{for } s=0 , \\ +\infty & \textnormal{otherwise.} \end{cases}ϕKL​(s)=⎩⎨⎧​slog(s)−s+11+∞​for s>0,for s=0,otherwise.​
(36)
Example: Total variation

With the convention of this book, total variation TV:=DϕTV\TV \eqdef \Divergm_{\phi_{\TV}}TV:=DϕTV​​ is the full variation norm, without the factor 1/21/21/2 sometimes used for probabilities. It is associated with

ϕTV(s)={∣s−1∣for s≥0,+∞otherwise.\phi_{\TV}(s)= \begin{cases} |s-1| & \textnormal{for } s\geq0 , \\ +\infty & \textnormal{otherwise.} \end{cases}ϕTV​(s)={∣s−1∣+∞​for s≥0,otherwise.​
(37)

It actually defines a norm on the full space of measures M(X)\Mm(\X)M(X) where

TV(α∣β)=∥α−β∥TV,where∥α∥TV=∣α∣(X)=∫X d∣α∣(x).\TV(\al|\be) = \norm{\al-\be}_{\TV}, \qquad\text{where}\qquad \norm{\al}_{\TV} = |\al|(\X) = \int_\X \d|\al|(x).TV(α∣β)=∥α−β∥TV​,where∥α∥TV​=∣α∣(X)=∫X​d∣α∣(x).
(38)

If α\alα has a density ρα\density{\al}ρα​ on X=Rd\X=\RR^\dimX=Rd, then the TV norm is the L1L^1L1 norm on functions, ∥α∥TV=∫X∣ρα(x)∣ dx=∥ρα∥L1\norm{\al}_{\TV} = \int_\X |\density{\al}(x)| \d x = \norm{\density{\al}}_{L^1}∥α∥TV​=∫X​∣ρα​(x)∣dx=∥ρα​∥L1​.

If α\alα is discrete as in (30), then the TV norm is the ℓ1\ell^1ℓ1 norm of vectors in Rn\RR^nRn, ∥α∥TV=∑i∣ai∣=∥a∥ℓ1\norm{\al}_{\TV}=\sum_i |\a_i| = \norm{\a}_{\ell^1}∥α∥TV​=∑i​∣ai​∣=∥a∥ℓ1​.

KL and total variation are two very different ϕ\phiϕ-divergences: the former is smooth and sensitive to density ratios, whereas the latter is a nonsmooth norm. Pinsker’s fundamental inequality nevertheless controls the square of the latter by the former Pinsker, 1964.

Theorem: Pinsker Inequality

Let α,β∈M+1(X)\alpha,\beta\in\Mm_+^1(\X)α,β∈M+1​(X) be probability measures on a measurable space. With the full-variation convention of (38),

TV(α∣β)2=∥α−β∥TV2≤2KL⁡(α∣β).\TV(\alpha\mid\beta)^2 = \norm{\alpha-\beta}_{\TV}^2 \leq 2\KL(\alpha\mid\beta).TV(α∣β)2=∥α−β∥TV2​≤2KL(α∣β).
(39)

On a finite space, for a,b∈Δna,b\in\simplex_na,b∈Δn​, this becomes

∥a−b∥ℓ12≤2KL⁡(a∣b).\norm{a-b}_{\ell^1}^2 \leq 2\operatorname{KL}(a\mid b).∥a−b∥ℓ12​≤2KL(a∣b).

a−b=12∥α−β∥TV.a-b=\frac12\norm{\alpha-\beta}_{\TV}.a−b=21​∥α−β∥TV​.

The resulting function has value and first derivative zero at a=ba=ba=b, while its second derivative is 1/a+1/(1−a)−4≥01/a+1/(1-a)-4\geq01/a+1/(1−a)−4≥0. Remark: Strong vs. weak topology

The total variation norm (38) defines the so-called “strong” topology on the space of measures.

For probability measures on a compact metric space,

W1(α,β)≤diam⁡(X)2∥α−β∥TV.\Wass_1(\al,\be) \leq \frac{\operatorname{diam}(\X)}{2}\norm{\al-\be}_{\TV}.W1​(α,β)≤2diam(X)​∥α−β∥TV​.
(43)

Indeed, a 1-Lipschitz test function can be shifted so that its sup norm is at most diam⁡(X)/2\operatorname{diam}(\X)/2diam(X)/2. Thus total-variation convergence implies weak convergence.

The converse is false: if xn→xx_n\to xxn​→x with xn≠xx_n\ne xxn​=x, then δxn⇀δx\delta_{x_n}\rightharpoonup\delta_xδxn​​⇀δx​ but ∥δxn−δx∥TV=2\norm{\delta_{x_n}-\delta_x}_{\TV}=2∥δxn​​−δx​∥TV​=2 for every nnn.

A chief advantage is that M+1(X)\Mm_+^1(\Xx)M+1​(X) (once again on a compact ground space X\XX) is compact for the weak topology so that from any sequence of probability measures (αk)k(\al_k)_k(αk​)k​, one can always extract a converging subsequence, which makes it a suitable space for several optimization problems.

The Hellinger divergence is often written with ϕH(s)=(s−1)2\phi_H(s)=(\sqrt{s}-1)^2ϕH​(s)=(s​−1)2. If α=ραλ\alpha=\rho_\alpha\lambdaα=ρα​λ and β=ρβλ\beta=\rho_\beta\lambdaβ=ρβ​λ, then Hellinger⁡(α,β)=∥ρα−ρβ∥L2(λ)\operatorname{Hellinger}(\alpha,\beta) =\norm{\sqrt{\rho_\alpha}-\sqrt{\rho_\beta}}_{L^2(\lambda)}Hellinger(α,β)=∥∥​ρα​​−ρβ​​∥∥​L2(λ)​. JS⁡(α,β)2=12KL⁡ ⁣(α|α+β2)+12KL⁡ ⁣(β|α+β2),\operatorname{JS}(\alpha,\beta)^2 = \frac12\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\alpha\middle|\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right) + \frac12\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\beta\middle|\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right),JS(α,β)2=21​KL(α∣∣​2α+β​)+21​KL(β∣∣​2α+β​),

and 0≤JS⁡(α,β)2≤log⁡20\le\operatorname{JS}(\alpha,\beta)^2\le\log20≤JS(α,β)2≤log2. Its exact generator is

Remark: ϕ\phiϕ-divergences versus Bregman divergences

Except for KL-type entropies, ϕ\phiϕ-divergences should not be confused with Bregman divergences. A ϕ\phiϕ-divergence compares measures pointwise through the density ratio  dα/ dβ\d\alpha/\d\betadα/dβ. It is invariant under measurable bijections and cannot increase under measurable coarse-graining or a Markov kernel Ciszár, 1967. A Bregman divergence is generated by a convex functional on a linear space and measures first-order Taylor error. KL is special because the integral entropy α↦∫ρlog⁡ρ\alpha\mapsto\int \rho\log\rhoα↦∫ρlogρ produces a Bregman divergence whose density-ratio form is also a ϕ\phiϕ-divergence.

Variational Dual Formula¶

The following formula turns a pointwise density-ratio penalty into a dual optimization problem over test functions. It is the analogue, for ϕ\phiϕ-divergences, of the Kantorovich dual formula for transport costs.

Proposition: Variational Representation of a ϕ\phiϕ-Divergence

Assume that X\XX is compact. Since ϕ\phiϕ is extended by +∞+\infty+∞ on negative arguments, define its Legendre transform by

ϕ∗(s):=sup⁡r≥0{sr−ϕ(r)}.\phi^*(s) \eqdef \sup_{r\ge0}\{sr-\phi(r)\}.ϕ∗(s):=r≥0sup​{sr−ϕ(r)}.
(47)

as

Dϕ(α∣β)=sup⁡f∈C(X){∫Xf(x)  dα(x)−∫Xϕ∗(f(x))  dβ(x)}.D_\phi(\alpha|\beta) = \sup_{f\in\Cc(\X)} \left\{ \int_\X f(x)\,\d\alpha(x) -\int_\X \phi^*(f(x))\,\d\beta(x) \right\}.Dϕ​(α∣β)=f∈C(X)sup​{∫X​f(x)dα(x)−∫X​ϕ∗(f(x))dβ(x)}.
(48)

Equivalently,

Dϕ∗(f∣β)=∫Xϕ∗(f(x))  dβ(x).D_\phi^*(f|\beta)=\int_\X \phi^*(f(x))\,\d\beta(x).Dϕ∗​(f∣β)=∫X​ϕ∗(f(x))dβ(x).
(49)
Proof

First assume ϕ∞′=+∞\phi'_\infty=+\inftyϕ∞′​=+∞, so the divergence is infinite unless α\alphaα has a density ρ≥0\rho\ge0ρ≥0 with respect to β\betaβ. The Legendre--Fenchel transform of Dϕ(⋅∣β)D_\phi(\cdot|\beta)Dϕ​(⋅∣β) is

Dϕ∗(f∣β)=sup⁡ρ≥0∫Xf(x)ρ(x)  dβ(x)−∫Xϕ(ρ(x))  dβ(x)=∫Xsup⁡ρ(x)≥0(f(x)ρ(x)−ϕ(ρ(x))) dβ(x).D_\phi^*(f|\beta) = \sup_{\rho\ge0} \int_\X f(x)\rho(x)\,\d\beta(x) - \int_\X\phi(\rho(x))\,\d\beta(x) = \int_\X \sup_{\rho(x)\ge0} \left(f(x)\rho(x)-\phi(\rho(x))\right) \d\beta(x).Dϕ∗​(f∣β)=ρ≥0sup​∫X​f(x)ρ(x)dβ(x)−∫X​ϕ(ρ(x))dβ(x)=∫X​ρ(x)≥0sup​(f(x)ρ(x)−ϕ(ρ(x)))dβ(x).
(50)

This is the displayed integral of ϕ∗\phi^*ϕ∗. For finite ϕ∞′\phi'_\inftyϕ∞′​, the upper endpoint of dom⁡ϕ∗\operatorname{dom}\phi^*domϕ∗ encodes the singular recession term. Convexity, weak-∗\ast∗ lower semicontinuity, and Fenchel--Moreau then give the dual expression.

GANs via Duality¶

GANs fit naturally into the dual viewpoint: the discriminator is a parameterized potential and the generator moves a reference measure. This section first explains the original divergence-based GAN objective, then contrasts it with integral probability metrics such as MMD and Wasserstein distances.

The goal is to fit a generative parametric model αθ=(gθ)♯ζ\alpha_\theta=(g_\theta)_\sharp\zetaαθ​=(gθ​)♯​ζ to empirical data

β=1m∑j=1mδyj,\beta=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_{y_j},β=m1​j=1∑m​δyj​​,
(51)

where ζ\zetaζ is a fixed probability measure on the latent space and gθ:Z→Xg_\theta:\mathcal{Z}\to\Xgθ​:Z→X is the generator, often a neural network.

Divergence-Based Adversarial Losses¶

Any ϕ\phiϕ-divergence can be written in adversarial form through the dual formula:

min⁡θDϕ(αθ∣β)=min⁡θsup⁡f{∫Xf  dαθ−Dϕ∗(f∣β)}=min⁡θsup⁡f{∫Zf(gθ(z))  dζ(z)−1m∑j=1mϕ∗(f(yj))}.\min_\theta D_\phi(\alpha_\theta|\beta) = \min_\theta\sup_f \left\{ \int_\X f\,\d\alpha_\theta - D_\phi^*(f|\beta) \right\} = \min_\theta\sup_f \left\{ \int_\mathcal{Z} f(g_\theta(z))\,\d\zeta(z) - \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\phi^*(f(y_j)) \right\}.θmin​Dϕ​(αθ​∣β)=θmin​fsup​{∫X​fdαθ​−Dϕ∗​(f∣β)}=θmin​fsup​{∫Z​f(gθ​(z))dζ(z)−m1​j=1∑m​ϕ∗(f(yj​))}.
(52)

Replacing the unrestricted potential fff by a neural network fξf_\xifξ​ gives a saddle problem

min⁡θmax⁡ξ∫Zfξ(gθ(z))  dζ(z)−1m∑j=1mϕ∗(fξ(yj)).\min_\theta\max_\xi \int_\mathcal{Z} f_\xi(g_\theta(z))\,\d\zeta(z) - \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\phi^*(f_\xi(y_j)).θmin​ξmax​∫Z​fξ​(gθ​(z))dζ(z)−m1​j=1∑m​ϕ∗(fξ​(yj​)).
(53)

For fixed θ\thetaθ, restricting the discriminator gives a lower bound on the exact divergence. This distinction is essential for empirical data: if β\betaβ is discrete and αθ\alpha_\thetaαθ​ is non-atomic, a superlinear divergence is +∞+\infty+∞, while the restricted objective can remain finite.

The original vanilla GAN Goodfellow et al., 2014 corresponds, up to an additive constant and discriminator reparametrization, to the unscaled Jensen--Shannon generator ϕ^JS⁡=2ϕJS⁡\widehat\phi_{\operatorname{JS}}=2\phi_{\operatorname{JS}}ϕ​JS​=2ϕJS​,

ϕ^JS⁡(s)=slog⁡s−(s+1)log⁡s+12,ϕ^JS⁡∗(u)=−log⁡(2−eu),u<log⁡2,\widehat\phi_{\operatorname{JS}}(s) = s\log s-(s+1)\log\frac{s+1}{2}, \qquad \widehat\phi_{\operatorname{JS}}^*(u) = -\log(2-e^u), \quad u<\log2,ϕ​JS​(s)=slogs−(s+1)log2s+1​,ϕ​JS∗​(u)=−log(2−eu),u<log2,
(54)

Thus Dϕ^JS⁡=2JS⁡2D_{\widehat\phi_{\operatorname{JS}}}=2\operatorname{JS}^2Dϕ​JS​​=2JS2. In practice the min--max problem is solved by alternating stochastic gradient descent/ascent. Although the unrestricted maximization is concave in fff, neural parametrization generally destroys concavity in ξ\xiξ; the generator problem is likewise nonconvex in θ\thetaθ. Density-ratio losses can also saturate on singular measures: JS⁡2\operatorname{JS}^2JS2 reaches its maximum log⁡2\log2log2 on disjoint supports.

Dual Norms and Integral Probability Metrics¶

Instead of a density-ratio divergence, one can minimize an integral probability metric:

min⁡θ∥αθ−β∥B=min⁡θsup⁡f∈B{∫Zf(gθ(z))  dζ(z)−1m∑j=1mf(yj)}.\min_\theta\norm{\alpha_\theta-\beta}_B = \min_\theta \sup_{f\in B} \left\{ \int_\mathcal{Z} f(g_\theta(z))\,\d\zeta(z) - \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m f(y_j) \right\}.θmin​∥αθ​−β∥B​=θmin​f∈Bsup​{∫Z​f(gθ​(z))dζ(z)−m1​j=1∑m​f(yj​)}.
(55)

MMD-GANs take BBB to be a unit ball in an RKHS Dziugaite et al., 2015; Wasserstein GANs take BBB to be a Lipschitz ball, following Kantorovich--Rubinstein duality Arjovsky et al., 2017Frogner et al., 2015. The advantage is topological: for a continuous kernel on a compact space, the RKHS unit ball is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, while the normalized Lipschitz ball is compact by Arzela--Ascoli. The objective is therefore weakly continuous. It can therefore compare singular empirical and generated measures through test functions instead of requiring pointwise density ratios. The price is that the discriminator class must be controlled geometrically, either by a kernel norm, a Lipschitz constraint, or a related regularization.

Remark: Weight clipping is only a proxy

Wasserstein GANs originally used weight clipping, constraining ∥ξ∥∞≤1\norm{\xi}_\infty\leq1∥ξ∥∞​≤1 as a proxy for enforcing fξ∈{f:Lip⁡(f)≤1}f_\xi\in\{f:\operatorname{Lip}(f)\leq1\}fξ​∈{f:Lip(f)≤1}. The parameter box is convex, but its image through a neural network is neither the full Lipschitz ball nor generally a convex function class, and parameter optimization remains nonconcave. Clipping is therefore a heuristic rather than a faithful implementation of the Kantorovich--Rubinstein constraint.

Example: Application to imitation learning

In imitation learning, one can compare the expert occupancy measure ρE\rho_EρE​ and the learner occupancy measure ρθ\rho_\thetaρθ​ on state-action space. OT gives either a primal matching loss W(ρθ,ρE)W(\rho_\theta,\rho_E)W(ρθ​,ρE​), or a dual adversarial reward obtained from a Kantorovich potential. Thus the discriminator in an adversarial imitation method can be interpreted as a learned reward shaping the learner toward the expert distribution, exactly as the GAN discriminator above is a learned potential. Wasserstein adversarial imitation and primal Wasserstein imitation exploit this distribution-matching viewpoint while retaining the geometry of state-action space, for instance through a cost that compares nearby states and actions more mildly than distant ones Xiao et al., 2019Dadashi et al., 2020.
